newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel inflation higher in '96 but trend is lower.
newsitem.headline: Israel inflation higher in '96 but trend is lower.

text.p: Israeli inflation rose to 10.6 percent in 1996, up from 8.1 percent in 1995, the Central Bureau of Statistics said on Wednesday, but analysts said the second half of the year saw a marked slowing trend.

Inflation was running at a 14.6 percent annualised pace in the first half of 1996, but in the second half the rate fell to half that, estimated Jonathan Katz, chief economist at Solid Financial Markets.

Analysts said a turnaround in housing prices was the single biggest factor in moderating inflation. Housing prices doubled in real terms over the previous eight years and were rising at an annualised rate of 23.1 percent in first-half 1996, according to Bank Hapoalim.
Katz estimated the rise in housing prices fell to an annualised rate of just four percent in the second half. For the full year, housing prices rose 14 percent.

The Bank of Israel's restrictive monetary policy, which saw short-term rates peak at 17 percent in the middle of last year, contributed, as did the strengthening of the shekel, which kept prices of imported products low.
"We ended the year with a stronger shekel in nominal terms than in June," Katz said.
Underlying inflation has taken a turn lower, as well. The Israeli producer price index rose 7.0 percent last year, compared with 10.0 percent in 1995.
Analysts were optimistic the moderating trend would continue into 1997.

"Inflation has entered the (government's) target zone of seven to 10 percent, and it is certainly under control," said Ptachia Bar Shavit, chief economist at Bank Hapoalim. Hapoalim is forecasting 8.5 inflation for all of 1997, with housing prices serving as a key moderating factor.
"We believe that housing prices will rise less than the index, about half or four percent," he said.
In the bond market, inflationary expectations for the next 12 months have declined steadily since November to 9.15 percent from around 12 percent in October.

Monetary restraint will continue to cool inflation as will the slowing economy. The Treasury expects gross domestic product to expand about four percent this year, down from an estimated 4.4 percent in 1996 and 7.1 percent in 1995.

Hezy Gutman, head of the economics department at First International Bank of Israel, said the only development he saw that could re-ignite inflation was a sharp depreciation in the shekel. He said that was unlikely to occur.

Although the trend in the second half was lower, economists and the market were disappointed by a relatively high December CPI. The index rose 0.8 percent, at the upper end of expectations, due to an unexpectedly sharp rise in housing prices for the month.

"The index is a little disappointing. It's at the top end of the range of expectations, but it's not terrible. I was not expecting the Bank of Israel to lower interest rates this month," said Baruch Glicksberg of Clal Insurance.
Shahar Gazit of Betucha Securities and Investments also expressed disappointment, saying he was expecting a rise of 0.6 to 0.7 percent.
The Bank of Israel is due to announce February interest rates on January 27. The base rate is currently 14.7 percent.
